topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: We propose a novel, geometrically-grounded method to isolate epistemic uncertainty in deep neural networks by analyzing the stability of topological features (persistent homology) in hierarchical latent spaces, explicitly distinguishing it from aleatoric uncertainty.

BACKGROUND: A core open problem in uncertainty quantification is the conflation of epistemic (model ignorance) and aleatoric (data noise) uncertainty. Current probabilistic methods often fail to provide interpretable, disentangled signals, especially for novel out-of-distribution (OOD) data types, which is critical for AI safety.

APPROACH: We will develop a Topological Uncertainty Score (TUS) based on the Wasserstein distance between the persistence diagram of a test batch and a layer-wise reference diagram from training data. Crucially, we theoretically justify and empirically validate that TUS remains low for in-distribution data with high label ambiguity (aleatoric uncertainty) but spikes for OOD data, due to topological instability in the latent manifold mapping. We implement scalable approximations for computational feasibility.

EXPERIMENT: Using CIFAR-10 (in-distribution), we test against: 1) OOD datasets (SVHN, Textures) for epistemic uncertainty, and 2) a curated set of ambiguous in-distribution images (e.g., dog-cat blends) for aleatoric uncertainty. We benchmark TUS against Bayesian/ensemble baselines and simpler latent metrics (Mahalanobis, k-NN density) in ablation, proving its unique signal. We validate score stability across multiple training runs.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond scalar variance measures by providing an interpretable, topological signature of *why* a model is uncertain, directly disentangling epistemic from aleatoric uncertainty based on latent manifold geometry, a distinction lacking in prior work.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: We propose to establish a causal theory linking epistemic uncertainty in deep neural networks to quantifiable distortions in the topology of their latent manifolds, and to develop efficient, perturbation-stable topological signatures for practical uncertainty quantification.

BACKGROUND: Current methods for distinguishing epistemic from aleatoric uncertainty in deep learning are often correlative, computationally expensive, or provide only aggregate measures. A fundamental, causal understanding of how a model's internal geometric structure reflects its knowledge is lacking, hindering the development of robust, interpretable uncertainty signals.

APPROACH: First, we will formalize the link by proving that under a manifold learning assumption, regions of high epistemic uncertainty correspond to areas where the data manifold is poorly learned, causing pathological folding or rarefaction in the latent space. We will validate this causality using synthetic data with known manifold geometry and epistemic uncertainty. Second, we will develop an efficient topological signature by combining a stable, gradient-based input perturbation scheme with a graph-based approximation of persistent homology (using the Vietoris-Rips complex on a landmark-subsampled local neighborhood) and intrinsic dimension estimation.

EXPERIMENT: We will test on a controlled synthetic dataset and standard benchmarks (CIFAR-10/100, CIFAR-10-C, SVHN), evaluating the causal theory via intervention experiments and benchmarking our signature against geometric baselines (softmax entropy, distance to k-NN, local intrinsic dimension) on OOD detection, calibration error, and correlation with deep ensemble disagreement.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond correlation to establish a causal geometric theory of epistemic uncertainty, and delivers a practical, computationally tractable method derived from that theory, unlike prior topological approaches which are purely observational and prohibitively expensive.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: We propose a theoretically grounded, scalable method to quantify epistemic uncertainty in deep neural networks by analyzing the topological connectivity and local intrinsic dimensionality of the latent feature manifold, explicitly disentangling it from aleatoric uncertainty.

BACKGROUND: A core open problem in uncertainty quantification is the reliable separation of epistemic (model ignorance) and aleatoric (data noise) uncertainty. Current probabilistic and geometric methods often conflate the two, leading to unreliable out-of-distribution detection and poor interpretability in safety-critical applications.

APPROACH: The method defines epistemic uncertainty via a sample's isolation from the *topological skeleton* of the in-distribution latent manifold, computed using an efficient approximation of 1D persistent homology on a k-nearest neighbor graph, combined with a robust estimator of Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID). This directly measures connectivity deficits and manifold collapse, which we theoretically justify as signatures of model ignorance, unlike density-based measures. A scalable inference-time algorithm computes a Topological Uncertainty Score (TUS) per sample.

EXPERIMENT: We validate disentanglement on controlled synthetic datasets and standard benchmarks (CIFAR-10/100 vs. SVHN, Textures), using metrics for OOD detection (AUROC) and, crucially, for separating epistemic/aleatoric uncertainty on in-distribution ambiguous samples and adversarial examples. We compare against Mahalanobis distance, ensemble variance, and predictive entropy.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond simple density or distance metrics by using topological invariants (persistent homology, LID) that are provably sensitive to global manifold structure and connectivity, providing a direct, interpretable geometric signature of epistemic uncertainty that is theoretically distinct from data ambiguity.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: We propose to quantify epistemic uncertainty in deep neural networks by detecting characteristic distortions in the topological structure of a dimensionality-reduced latent space, benchmarking against strong geometric baselines to isolate the unique signal of model ignorance.

BACKGROUND: A key open problem is distinguishing epistemic from aleatoric uncertainty, especially for out-of-distribution detection. Current probabilistic methods often conflate these types or lack interpretability, failing to explain *why* a prediction is uncertain.

APPROACH: We will apply persistent homology to class-conditional PCA projections of a network's penultimate layer. The core hypothesis is that epistemic uncertainty manifests as statistically significant deviations in the persistence diagrams (e.g., birth/death of homology features) of these projections, which provide complementary information to density-based baselines like Mahalanobis distance. We will formally justify this by linking specific topological changes (e.g., fragmentation of a class manifold) to model confusion on synthetic data with isolated shift types.

EXPERIMENT: Using a ResNet-50 trained on CIFAR-10, we will test on controlled shifts (e.g., CIFAR-10-C for aleatoric, CIFAR-100 for epistemic) and measure OOD detection AUC. We will benchmark the Wasserstein distance of persistence diagrams against Mahalanobis and k-NN density on the same projection, demonstrating robustness across training seeds.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond scalar uncertainty scores to a geometric, interpretable signature of model confusion. It explicitly isolates the topological component of epistemic uncertainty by comparing against and augmenting strong geometric baselines on identical latent representations.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: We will quantify epistemic uncertainty by tracking the stability of the latent manifold's topology during training using scalable graph-based persistent homology, and directly link this training signal to inference-time uncertainty via a novel projection and local complexity score.

BACKGROUND: Current uncertainty quantification methods often conflate epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty, producing scores that are difficult to diagnose for model improvement. A core open problem is finding an interpretable, architecture-agnostic signature of a model's failure to form coherent internal representations, which is the root of epistemic uncertainty.

APPROACH: We propose monitoring the training dynamics of latent space topology as a diagnostic. To ensure tractability, we will compute persistent homology using a Vietoris-Rips filtration on a k-nearest neighbor graph constructed from per-class prototype embeddings, sampled at strategic training intervals. To isolate the epistemic signal, we will theoretically link topological instability (persistent "flickering" of H1 loops) to the model's unresolved representational ambiguity, and validate this against controlled ablations. Finally, we bridge to inference by projecting a test point into this graph and measuring the local topological complexity (e.g., change in cycle structure) its addition induces.

EXPERIMENT: We will train ensembles on mixed-domain datasets (CIFAR-10 + Textures) and correlate the variance of late-training topological metrics (e.g., lifetime of significant H1 cycles) with standard epistemic uncertainty measures (ensemble disagreement) on a hold-out set, demonstrating superior guidance for active learning loops compared to entropy-based baselines.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond statistical output analysis to a geometric analysis of the learning process itself, using scalable topological summaries as a direct, causal diagnostic for representational uncertainty, which prior variance-based methods cannot isolate.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA: Develop a foundation model that learns a causal, multi-modal latent dynamics manifold from unpaired temporal population data to predict and prescribe interventions for steering single-cell trajectories.

BACKGROUND: Current models for cellular dynamics (e.g., RNA velocity, neural ODEs) are typically unimodal, trained on perfectly paired data, or lack a framework for causal intervention. The open problem is to integrate asynchronous, multi-omic snapshots into a unified model that can distinguish correlation from causation and prescribe perturbations to achieve a target cell state.

APPROACH: We will train a transformer with a theoretically-grounded, masked imputation objective on large-scale, unpaired time-series data (scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq, live-cell imaging). The model will learn to infer a latent ODE system and an "intervention operator" that maps perturbations (e.g., drugs, knockouts) to shifts in this manifold, using techniques from causal representation learning to handle confounding.

EXPERIMENT: We will validate via iterative, closed-loop experimentation: the model will predict intermediate phenotypes and optimal perturbations to reprogram fibroblasts to cardiomyocytes; these predictions will be tested in wet-lab assays, and the resulting *unseen* experimental outcomes will be fed back to assess and refine the model's causal fidelity.

NOVELTY: The novelty is the integration of unpaired, multi-modal data into a prescriptive causal framework, moving beyond descriptive trajectory inference to learn a perturbation-aware dynamics model that can be iteratively refined with real-world experiments.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA: Develop a causal graph transformer, trained on perturbation-augmented spatial transcriptomic data, to predict how controlled combinations of neighboring cell types combinatorially instruct specific fibroblast activation states in lung fibrosis.

BACKGROUND: In pulmonary fibrosis, the transition of fibroblasts to pathological states is driven by complex signals from neighboring epithelial and immune cells, but the precise combinatorial rules of this niche instruction remain unknown. Current spatial models identify correlations but cannot predict the causal effect of specific, controllable niche configurations on cell fate.

APPROACH: We will train a model where the input is a controllable niche graph—nodes defined by experimentally-tunable cell types (e.g., alveolar epithelial, macrophage) and edges by physical adjacency—and the output is the predicted transcriptional state of a central fibroblast. The model will be pre-trained on published spatial transcriptomic data from fibrotic lung tissues, augmented with *in silico* perturbations of ligand-receptor pairs, and explicitly fine-tuned on new co-culture perturbation data (e.g., using ligand inhibitors).

EXPERIMENT: We will validate the model by physically constructing its top-predicted niche combinations to induce or suppress fibroblast activation in a micropatterned co-culture assay, then comparing the predicted and measured (via scRNA-seq) fibroblast states using a precision-recall metric for activation gene programs.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond correlative spatial graphs by training on perturbation data to infer causal niche grammar, and its input/output is designed for direct experimental testing with controllable cellular inputs, enabling closed-loop hypothesis generation and validation.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA: Develop a foundation model that learns a causally regularized latent space from paired single-cell perturbation data, enabling the prediction of combinatorial interventions for targeted cellular state transitions.

BACKGROUND: Current single-cell foundation models create powerful embeddings but lack actionable links to experimental perturbations. The core challenges are the scarcity of high-quality paired perturbation data and the inability of models to generalize causal effects beyond their training distribution, limiting their utility for designing cellular reprogramming experiments.

APPROACH: We will train a transformer using a novel three-stage curriculum: first on static atlases, then on a newly curated unified dataset of paired perturbation profiles (leveraging standardized multiplexed screens like Perturb-seq), and finally with a causal invariance objective that penalizes sensitivity to batch variables. The architecture will use state-dependent linear operators to model nonlinear, context-specific perturbation effects.

EXPERIMENT: We will validate the model by predicting perturbations to shift primary human macrophages from a pro-inflammatory (M1) to an anti-inflammatory (M2) state, using a predefined transcriptomic signature and functional assay (phagocytosis) as benchmarks. Predictions will be tested against a random baseline and a literature-derived cocktail in a bounded Perturb-seq experiment.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior models that learn associative embeddings, this framework explicitly models perturbation effects as potentially nonlinear and context-dependent, and its training is designed for causal identifiability and out-of-distribution generalization across cell types and conditions.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA: To build a foundation model that predicts single-cell perturbation responses by explicitly learning how core response programs are modulated by distinct, interpretable biological contexts like spatial neighborhood and transcriptional history.

BACKGROUND: A major limitation in predicting perturbation effects is the failure to model how a cell's specific microenvironment—its spatial neighbors and recent state history—shapes its response. Current models treat cell types as static, missing the context-dependent variation crucial for understanding tissue-level drug action or disease mechanisms.

APPROACH: We will pre-train a transformer on large-scale perturbation atlases (e.g., Perturb-seq) to learn core cell-intrinsic response programs. For context-awareness, we will implement a modular encoding branch where distinct, biologically justified context vectors (e.g., from neighborhood graphs or pseudo-temporal trajectories) are integrated via a causal fine-tuning framework on smaller, paired datasets, rigorously controlling for confounders.

EXPERIMENT: We will benchmark the model using controlled *in silico* tasks on existing data (e.g., predicting differential drug response across tissue sites) and validate with a definitive *ex vivo* context-swap experiment in organoids, where cells of the same lineage are exposed to different niches, followed by Perturb-seq to establish causal context effects.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond context-agnostic prediction by using a modular, interpretable architecture to disentangle and quantify the specific contribution of defined contextual factors, enabled by a causality-aware training strategy that does not require perfectly paired multi-modal data.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA: Develop a multimodal foundation model for single-cell biology that learns to integrate transcriptomic, epigenomic, and protein data by leveraging spatial context as a conditional, rather than absolute, signal for cross-modal imputation and perturbation response prediction.

BACKGROUND: Current models fail to perform accurate, joint imputation across fundamentally mismatched single-cell modalities (e.g., RNA from one cell, ATAC from another) without shared measurements. This limits the construction of complete cellular maps. Spatial coordinates provide a probabilistic constraint for this alignment, as neighboring cells are more likely to share states, but existing tools treat spatial graphs as fixed truth, ignoring technical gaps and biological noise.

APPROACH: We will pre-train a transformer with modality-specific encoders using a two-stage objective: first, a contrastive loss aligns cells from different modalities within a shared embedding using spatial neighborhood overlap as a weak supervisory signal; second, a masked prediction task reconstructs one modality from another, where the spatial graph from the *available* modality informs cross-modal attention weights. This explicitly models spatial context as a noisy, data-dependent prior.

EXPERIMENT: We will benchmark on curated, real perturbation datasets (e.g., Perturb-seq with imaging or spatial transcriptomics) where held-out experimental conditions are predicted. Primary metrics: accuracy of cross-modal state prediction for perturbed cells (e.g., RNA from ATAC) and correlation of predicted neighbor responses against measured spatial transcriptomics post-perturbation.

NOVELTY: Unlike modular alignment pipelines or models requiring perfectly matched data, this is an end-to-end foundation model that learns a unified representation from mismatched atlases by formally treating spatial proximity as a probabilistic guide for multimodal integration, directly enabling prediction of perturbation responses across modalities.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: To predict the populations of pre-existing conformational states in proteins by developing a maximum entropy model that directly maps co-evolutionary covariance, after correcting for phylogenetic and static constraints, to a quantitative free energy landscape.

BACKGROUND: AlphaFold predicts a single, static structure, but many proteins function through an equilibrium of discrete conformational states (e.g., active/inactive). The core open problem is to quantitatively predict the free energy differences between these known states from sequence alone, moving beyond structure prediction to conformational population prediction.

APPROACH: First, we will develop a method to isolate the dynamic component of co-evolutionary signals by subtracting the covariance attributable to the static fold (inferred from AlphaFold2 predictions) and phylogenetic relationships. This purified covariance matrix will then constrain a maximum entropy model to generate a minimal ensemble of structures, whose state populations are determined by fitting to the statistical energy landscape derived from sequence data.

EXPERIMENT: We will test the model on proteins with NMR or DEER data quantifying state populations (e.g., GPCRs, kinases), using the primary metric of predicted vs. experimental free energy differences (ΔΔG) between wild-type and point mutants known to shift conformational equilibria.

NOVELTY: Unlike methods that assume co-evolution directly reports dynamics, this approach rigorously disentangles static and dynamic covariance and provides a biophysical, testable link between sequence statistics and quantitative state populations, not just structural diversity.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: To develop a physics-informed, contrastive latent diffusion model that learns a data-driven conformational manifold from static structures, enabling the prediction of functionally relevant, energetically plausible alternative states conditioned on biological triggers.

BACKGROUND: AlphaFold provides accurate static folds but cannot predict the conformational dynamics essential for function, such as allosteric transitions or induced-fit binding. The critical open problem is to infer the accessible, functional energy landscape from a single static snapshot, which requires moving beyond structure generation to modeling physically realistic transitions.

APPROACH: We will train a geometric graph neural network with a hybrid loss function combining a contrastive objective on multi-conformation PDB data with explicit physical priors (e.g., Rosetta torsional potentials and steric clash penalties). This model will learn to map a starting structure to a latent manifold of plausible conformations, from which a diffusion process can sample specific, conditioned transitions (e.g., upon ligand binding).

EXPERIMENT: Stage 1 validation will test the model's ability to rank known alternative conformations over decoys for held-out proteins, using metrics like correlation with experimental NMR S² order parameters. Stage 2 will involve testing a single high-confidence novel prediction—such as a cryptic pocket opening—using a cost-effective biophysical assay like DEER spectroscopy to measure the predicted distance change.

NOVELTY: Unlike pure generative models or molecular dynamics, this method explicitly integrates physical constraints into a data-driven manifold learning framework, shifting the goal from sampling arbitrary dynamics to predicting the subset of thermodynamically accessible, functionally relevant states.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: Develop a deep learning model that predicts functionally relevant protein conformational ensembles by integrating regularized higher-order co-evolutionary statistics with physics-based simulations, trained and validated on a zero-shot, leakage-proof benchmark.

BACKGROUND: AlphaFold2 provides static snapshots but fails to predict the conformational ensembles essential for function. The open problem is to move from a single structure to a predictive model of the population-weighted landscape of alternative states using only sequence information and one known structure.

APPROACH: We will train a model on protein families with multiple known PDB states, using a novel architecture that inputs: 1) higher-order co-evolutionary features, regularized via a pairwise-informed prior to function with standard-depth alignments, and 2) collective variables derived from short, enhanced-sampling MD simulations. The model will be trained to predict discrete alternative states and their relative populations, not by interpolating between known states, but by learning a mapping from sequence-and-dynamics-derived features to ensemble properties.

EXPERIMENT: We will perform rigorous zero-shot validation: the model is trained on proteins with multiple known states, then tested on held-out proteins where only one state is in the PDB, comparing predictions against experimental NMR/DEER data. A foundational benchmark on simulated ensembles from AF2-MD will quantify accuracy where the ground truth is known.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond pairwise co-evolution to explicitly link regularized higher-order statistics to ensemble thermodynamics, and provides a principled integration framework where evolutionary constraints are used to bias—and be refined by—physics-based simulations, rather than an ad hoc combination.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: Develop a deep learning model that predicts how applied forces and non-equilibrium cellular conditions redistribute a protein’s conformational ensemble by training on computationally generated ensembles and validating with targeted single-molecule experiments.

BACKGROUND: AlphaFold predicts static, equilibrium structures but cannot forecast how functional conformational landscapes are reshaped under active cellular conditions like shear force or motor protein pulling. This limits understanding in mechanobiology and allosteric regulation, where non-equilibrium fluxes populate rare, functionally critical states.

APPROACH: A hybrid training strategy will be used: a foundational model with a "condition encoder" for force/pressure inputs will be primarily trained on diverse, computationally generated conformational ensembles from molecular dynamics simulations under applied forces. This large-scale data will be sparsely refined and validated using high-fidelity experimental ensembles from HS-AFM and single-molecule FRET under load for a curated set of mechanosensitive proteins.

EXPERIMENT: The model will be validated via blind predictions on proteins like titin under unseen force protocols, with predictions compared to new single-molecule experiments that include systematic controls for linkers and force application methods to ensure biological generality.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond single-structure prediction to a generalizable, condition-dependent ensemble model, distinct from force-biased simulations by learning an evolutionary-informed mapping from force to population shifts across folds, trained at scale on computational data.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: Develop a deep learning model that predicts a protein’s conformational ensemble as a function of a specific, controllable non-equilibrium variable: the vectorial translation speed at which it is synthesized.

BACKGROUND: AlphaFold predicts static, equilibrium structures but cannot capture how non-equilibrium cellular processes, like translation, shape functional conformational ensembles. A critical open problem is predicting how co-translational folding dynamics, dictated by ribosome speed, determine a protein’s final structural distribution and functional state.

APPROACH: Train a conditional diffusion model on experimental structures from the PDB and NMR-derived ensembles, directly conditioned on discrete, experimentally tunable translation speed parameters (e.g., slow, medium, fast). The model will learn to interpolate and extrapolate from a limited set of proteins with conformational data linked to specific translation rates, generated via in vitro ribosome profiling and subsequent structural characterization.

EXPERIMENT: Validate by predicting distinct ensembles for a held-out protein synthesized at slow vs. fast speeds, and test these predictions against experimental ensembles determined by in-cell NMR or single-molecule FRET under precisely controlled translation conditions.

NOVELTY: Unlike equilibrium ensemble predictors or generative models like RFdiffusion, this model is explicitly conditioned on a quantifiable non-equilibrium variable (translation speed) to predict context-dependent structural distributions, moving beyond the "one sequence, one structure" paradigm.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA: Develop a scalable, mini-batch topological regularization loss for deep generative models that enforces geometric fidelity between data and latent space by comparing their persistent homology via a normalized, density-aware metric.

BACKGROUND: Deep generative models often induce topological distortions (e.g., false holes, bridges) in their latent spaces, degrading sample quality and latent interpretability. Current topological methods in ML are primarily diagnostic; a framework to actively prevent these distortions during training is lacking.

APPROACH: We will implement a differentiable TopoReg loss using mini-batch persistent homology. To ensure meaningful cross-space comparison, we will normalize point clouds by their intrinsic dimensionality and use a density-adaptive filtration scale. Computational feasibility will be achieved via an efficient approximation of the Sliced Wasserstein distance on persistence diagrams and a caching strategy for a stable topological "anchor" derived from a fixed data subset.

EXPERIMENT: We will benchmark TopoReg-VAEs/GANs against baselines on synthetic manifolds (tori, spheres) and image datasets (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST), evaluating via topological distortion scores, FID, and the coherence of latent interpolations.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond topological diagnostics to an integrated, trainable regularizer, introducing a normalized comparison protocol to validly align topological features across spaces of differing scale and density.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA: We propose a causal framework that uses persistent homology to measure the stability of topological features in a model's latent space under task-relevant perturbations, and we test if engineering this stability improves model robustness.

BACKGROUND: A core vulnerability in machine learning is that models learn brittle, local correlations from high-dimensional data rather than robust, global structures. Current robustness metrics fail to characterize the stability of the intrinsic geometric manifold that a model's representations form, which is where decisions are made.

APPROACH: We will define Topological Resilience Score (TRS) as the persistence of homology features in a network's latent representations under a canonical set of adversarial and augmentation-based perturbations. We will then design a topologically-aware regularization loss that directly maximizes TRS during training to engineer more robust feature manifolds.

EXPERIMENT: Using synthetic datasets with controlled topological invariants and real-world benchmarks, we will conduct ablation studies to isolate the causal effect of TRS on robustness, comparing it against baselines like margin and dimensionality, and measure downstream performance on adversarial and out-of-distribution tests.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond correlational analysis of data topology to a causal, intervention-based study of feature-space topology, introducing a direct method to optimize the topological stability of learned representations for robustness.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA: We propose a theoretical and empirical framework that quantifies the adversarial robustness of deep neural networks by analyzing the stability of persistent homology profiles computed directly on high-dimensional activation vectors, linking topological instability to vulnerability via the geometric distortion of the data manifold.

BACKGROUND: A fundamental open problem is understanding why neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial perturbations. Current robustness metrics lack intrinsic, geometric explanations, and most topological data analysis (TDA) applications to neural networks rely on unstable dimensionality reduction, obscuring the true relationship between a network's internal geometry and its robustness.

APPROACH: To avoid the instability of dimensionality reduction, we will compute persistent homology directly on sparse Vietoris-Rips filtrations of high-dimensional activation point clouds using efficient cohomology algorithms and the Wasserstein distance. We will ground our hypothesis by formally linking the persistence of homological features across perturbation scales to the local Lipschitz constant of the layer mapping, predicting that robust networks exhibit more stable persistence profiles.

EXPERIMENT: We will train controlled pairs of standard and adversarially robust networks (e.g., on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100) with matched architecture and random seeds, compute persistence profiles for clean and adversarial batches at multiple layers, and rigorously test if profile stability (measured via bottleneck distance) correlates with and predicts robust accuracy under PGD attack, controlling for all non-robustness factors.

NOVELTY: This work moves beyond heuristic Betti number comparisons and unstable visualizations by employing direct, stable homology computations on activations and providing a novel theoretical link between persistence stability and Lipschitzness, enabling a causal, controlled experimental design to isolate topology as a signal of robustness.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA: We propose a novel, causally-grounded method to quantify the local topological complexity of a neural network's latent representations as a predictive measure of its robustness to adversarial attacks and distributional shift.

BACKGROUND: A core open problem in deep learning is understanding why models fail on out-of-distribution data. While global topological data analysis has been applied, we lack a causal, mechanistic link between the local topological structure of learned representations—specifically, the prevalence of high-dimensional holes in activation space neighborhoods—and a model's empirical fragility.

APPROACH: To overcome the curse of dimensionality, we will compute persistent homology on the intrinsic low-dimensional coordinates of local activation neighborhoods, obtained via UMAP. We will establish causality by benchmarking against the topology of the corresponding input data patches and against synthetic networks with controlled fragility. The final metric will be a stable, layer-wise measure of persistent entropy normalized by null models.

EXPERIMENT: We will correlate this normalized topological metric against adversarial (PGD) and corruption (CIFAR-10-C) accuracy across models with known robustness differences (standard, adversarial, and contrastively trained), using statistical significance testing to move beyond mere correlation.

NOVELTY: This work shifts focus from the global topology of data manifolds to the causal analysis of local topological complexity in *learned representations*, providing an interpretable, intrinsic-dimension-aware metric for robustness prediction.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA: We will develop a scalable topological pipeline to causally measure and then minimize adversarial-induced phase transitions in the latent shape of neural representations, moving beyond correlation to establish topology as a fundamental driver of robustness.

BACKGROUND: Deep neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial perturbations, but explanations based on local geometry lack a global, structural perspective. Prior topological data analysis (TDA) studies have shown correlations but failed to isolate topological change as a causal mechanism or provide scalable, layer-specific diagnostics for high-dimensional activations.

APPROACH: We will introduce a computationally feasible TDA pipeline using persistent homology on dimension-reduced activations from critical layers, identified via intrinsic dimension estimation. To establish causality, we will contrast adversarial effects against rigorous baselines (clean data variation, random noise) and perform sample-level spatiotemporal analysis of topological distortion versus misclassification. Finally, we will implement a differentiable topological regularizer, derived from persistence landscapes, that penalizes the premature death of homology features associated with class separation.

EXPERIMENT: Using ResNets and Vision Transformers on CIFAR-10/100, we will compute layer-wise persistence diagrams (H0, H1) for clean and PGD/AutoAttack-generated point clouds, quantifying distortion via Wasserstein distance to a clean baseline and correlating it with sample-level misclassification dynamics across layers.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely isolates topological phase transitions as a causal antecedent to misclassification, provides a scalable layer-wise diagnostic protocol, and advances a theoretically justified, differentiable topological regularizer focused on homology feature persistence beyond connected components.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA: This research establishes a paradigm for ultra-low-energy neuromorphic computing by theoretically and experimentally demonstrating that a memristive crossbar network can be trained to operate at its intrinsic stochastic resonance peak, where device noise becomes a computational resource for reliable sub-threshold (<100mV) signal processing.

BACKGROUND: The dominant energy cost in neuromorphic systems is static power dissipation from operating transistors above threshold voltage to ensure signal integrity. A fundamental open problem is overcoming the precision-efficiency trade-off. This work addresses it by shifting from noise suppression to noise exploitation, mirroring the stochastic efficiency of biological neural systems.

APPROACH: First, a theoretical framework will model the network's collective dynamics, proving a stable, tunable stochastic resonance (SR) regime exists under non-stationary noise and parasitics. Second, a "noise-adapted" learning rule will be developed in simulation to converge network weights to this SR peak. Finally, a custom 32x32 HfO₂ memristor array with precision sub-threshold control will experimentally validate the approach, with a full system energy budget analysis comparing total overhead to a deterministic, supra-threshold baseline.

EXPERIMENT: The network will be trained on MNIST using the noise-adapted rule, with success quantified by classification accuracy and energy per synaptic operation (fJ/spike), critically controlling for ensemble averaging effects and benchmarking against the deterministic high-signal mode on the same hardware.

NOVELTY: Prior work uses noise tolerantly or suppresses it; this is the first to propose and demonstrate a learning rule that actively tunes a memristive network to its optimal noise level for computation, creating a formal partnership between stochastic device physics and algorithmic training for energy efficiency.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA: We propose to engineer stochastic resonance in a diffusive memristor network by applying uniform, tunable noise to enable reliable sub-threshold neuromorphic computation, transforming noise from a detriment into a computational resource.

BACKGROUND: A core problem in neuromorphic hardware is the energy penalty of operating devices above their deterministic switching threshold. Current designs suppress noise, but this mandates high operational voltages, creating a fundamental trade-off between reliability and energy efficiency that limits scalability.

APPROACH: We will develop a minimal theoretical model of a coupled memristor network to simulate noise-enhanced signal propagation, then fabricate a 1D chain of diffusive memristors (Ag/SiO\(_x\)). A globally applied, calibrated white noise voltage will serve as the uniform stochastic field, while a weak sub-threshold signal is injected at the input node. Computational fidelity will be measured in real-time via the spectral power amplification of a known frequency component at the output node.

EXPERIMENT: We will test the system on a weak periodic pulse detection task, sweeping the noise intensity to identify a resonance peak in output signal quality. Critical controls include measuring single-device response, applying deterministic sub-threshold drives, and using random input signals to confirm the effect requires both the network, the structured input, and tuned noise.

NOVELTY: This work moves beyond single-device stochastic resonance by explicitly engineering a network-level coherent effect, and it introduces a practical, real-time spectral metric for computational fidelity that does not require offline averaging or perfect system knowledge.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA: Engineer a solid-state Stochastic Ionic Memristor (SIM) with nanostructured electrodes to create a programmable probabilistic switch, enabling energy-efficient sampling and Bayesian inference directly in neuromorphic hardware.

BACKGROUND: A key bottleneck in neuromorphic computing is the high energy cost of generating the tunable stochasticity required for probabilistic reasoning, which is typically synthesized digitally or with noisy analog circuits. This project addresses the open problem by developing a hardware primitive where stochasticity is an intrinsic, low-energy material property derived from controlled ion dynamics.

APPROACH: We will fabricate SIM devices using amorphous TaOₓ with mobile Ag⁺ ions and nanoporous Au electrodes designed via a kinetic Monte Carlo model to yield a specific distribution of ion activation energies. This model will guide electrode fabrication to achieve a target, voltage-tunable switching probability, moving beyond trial-and-error.

EXPERIMENT: We will statistically characterize intrinsic stochasticity using a 100-device array and a pulsed read-write-verify protocol with baseline correction, collecting >10⁴ events per device to map voltage to switching probability, while using *in-situ* TEM selectively to validate the modeled ion dynamics.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior memristors that suppress variability, we deliberately engineer electrode nanostructures to control stochastic switching, transforming it into a programmable computational resource rather than a device imperfection.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA: We propose a phononic neuromorphic network that uses surface acoustic waves (SAW) for spike transmission and phase-change-tuned nanomechanical resonators for synaptic weighting, aiming to achieve sub-10 aJ/spike operation by fundamentally redesigning the energy budget and addressing signal integrity and fabrication limits.

BACKGROUND: The energy efficiency of neuromorphic hardware is dominated by the capacitive charging of metallic interconnects for spike communication, not synaptic computation. Current approaches using electrons or even photons for on-chip signaling face fundamental thermodynamic and material loss bottlenecks that prevent attojoule-scale operation per spike event.

APPROACH: We will design a network of piezoelectric nanomechanical resonators on lithium niobate, where neurons emit frequency-encoded SAW spikes. Synaptic weights are stored in the mechanical domain by using a germanium-antimony-tellurium (GST) patch to strain-tune each resonator's frequency, altering its receptivity to incoming SAWs. To meet the energy target, we will employ a pulsed optomechanical readout scheme operating at the quantum-enhanced limit at 4K, where a single-photon-counting superconducting nanowire single-photon detector (SNSPD) detects spike-induced resonator motion, minimizing optical power overhead.

EXPERIMENT: We will fabricate a 5x5 resonator array with integrated GST synapses and characterize the system by implementing a 4-neuron winner-take-all circuit, measuring the total energy per spike event via calibrated optomechanical readout and verifying synaptic reconfiguration through GST phase transitions.

NOVELTY: This moves the entire spike propagation and weighting problem into the low-loss phononic domain and introduces a non-volatile, mechanical weight cell, unlike prior electronic or photonic neuromorphic systems, while its design is explicitly constrained by a full system-level energy budget and scalability model.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA: To achieve ultra-low-energy neuromorphic computation, this research co-designs spiking neural network algorithms with the intrinsic, non-stationary noise of memristive arrays operated in the sub-threshold regime, using adaptive inference to harness stochastic dynamics for reliable probabilistic computation.

BACKGROUND: A fundamental barrier to energy-efficient neuromorphic hardware is the high voltage required to overcome device noise for deterministic operation. This work addresses the open problem of performing reliable computation with the inherently stochastic and variable signals present at the minimal energy, sub-threshold operating point of nanoscale memristors.

APPROACH: We will develop a theoretical framework for a network of stochastic neurons, formally modeling computation via time-dependent switching probabilities. An adaptive co-design framework will then be implemented, where online noise characterization and spatial/temporal correlation mapping dynamically inform algorithm inference to compensate for device variability and drift, rather than assuming static noise profiles.

EXPERIMENT: We will benchmark a prototype memristive SNN on event-based gesture recognition, rigorously comparing accuracy and total system energy (including measurement overhead) against a high-voltage deterministic mode on the same hardware, while analyzing performance degradation with array scaling.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond prior stochastic computing by formally co-opting non-stationary, device-specific noise as a computational resource through adaptive algorithms, rather than seeking to suppress noise or relying on idealized, tunable stochastic resonance.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: Develop a conditional graph diffusion model to generate synthetically feasible, multi-target drug candidates from a privileged scaffold, explicitly optimized for a tunable activity profile across a defined target panel.

BACKGROUND: Current generative models for polypharmacology treat off-target effects as noise and rely on idealized, sparse activity data, leading to molecules with poor synthetic feasibility and unvalidated systems-level context. This project addresses the need for a practical, scaffold-centric AI that designs molecules with deliberate, tunable multi-target potency within a realistic chemical series.

APPROACH: The model will be a conditional discrete diffusion model trained on analogs of a privileged scaffold (e.g., aminopyrimidine for kinases). It will be conditioned on a desired activity vector and a simplified, ablatable context embedding from a GNN pre-trained on a target-pathway knowledge graph. The output will be novel, synthetically accessible molecules within the scaffold's chemical space.

EXPERIMENT: We will synthesize one top-ranked generated molecule and rigorously test it against the primary target panel and key off-targets (e.g., hERG), comparing it to a physical combination of benchmark single-target analogs from the same scaffold. An ablation study will quantitatively compare the full model to a baseline conditioned only on the activity vector and scaffold SMILES, using metrics of novelty, predicted multi-target activity, and docking scores.

NOVELTY: This work shifts from generating de novo polypharmacology from sparse data to the tunable, scaffold-constrained design of practical drug candidates, with validation anchored by a definitive single-molecule synthesis and a direct experimental comparison to a combination therapy benchmark.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: Develop a generative AI model that designs synthetically accessible small molecules with predefined, potent activity against a focused set of 2–3 biologically linked protein targets by explicitly conditioning on their structural contexts and multi-target activity profiles.

BACKGROUND: Current generative models for polypharmacology treat multi-target activity as a sum of independent objectives, often producing molecules that are synthetically intractable or lack a validated, balanced potency profile. The open problem is the integrated, context-aware design of molecules that are both synthetically feasible and exhibit deliberate, potent engagement with a specific combination of targets.

APPROACH: A diffusion model will generate molecules conditioned on a quantifiable multi-target activity vector (e.g., Ki < 100 nM for each target) and structural descriptors of the target binding sites. Synthesizability is enforced by integrating a forward synthesis predictor as a hard constraint during the graph generation process, ensuring every proposed step corresponds to a likely chemical reaction.

EXPERIMENT: The model will be trained on curated polypharmacology data for a defined target pair (e.g., BTK and JAK2). Validation will follow a strict cascade: first, computational docking and binding affinity prediction (MM/GBSA) against both targets; second, synthesis and testing of top candidates in biochemical binding assays (e.g., SPR) to confirm dual-target engagement at the specified potency thresholds.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond multi-objective optimization by using explicit, quantifiable multi-target activity thresholds and protein structural context as joint conditioning inputs, while directly embedding synthetic tractability as a non-negotiable constraint within the generative process.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: Develop a conditional diffusion model that generates synthesizable small molecules optimized for a fixed, expert-defined polypharmacology profile against 2–4 disease-relevant targets, using a Pareto-aware multi-objective framework for balanced affinity, selectivity, and ADMET properties.

BACKGROUND: Current generative models for molecular design fail to adequately address polypharmacology, as they typically optimize for single targets or use simplistic scalarized rewards for multiple objectives. This creates a gap in reliably producing novel, synthesizable drugs that deliberately and optimally modulate established multi-target mechanisms for complex diseases.

APPROACH: The model conditions generation on a fixed, curated target set representing a clear disease hypothesis. During fine-tuning, a Pareto-ranking strategy explicitly handles trade-offs between distinct oracles (binding affinity, selectivity, synthesizability, ADMET). To ensure robustness, oracle uncertainty quantification and a hold-out experimental dataset guard against reward hacking and overfitting to flawed predictions.

EXPERIMENT: We will generate a batch of 20 novel compounds for a defined target suite (e.g., for Alzheimer's: BACE1, GSK-3β, TLR4), alongside 10 controls from baseline models and 10 random decoys. Success requires statistically significant superiority in achieving pre-specified multi-target potency and selectivity thresholds across the batch in blinded in vitro assays, prior to any synthesis commitment.

NOVELTY: This work integrates a fixed, biologically-grounded polypharmacology hypothesis with a rigorous Pareto-optimization framework during generation, and validates model performance through a pre-defined, multi-compound statistical benchmark against controls, moving beyond single-compound validation.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: A generative AI framework that co-designs small molecules and stabilized protein conformations by conditioning on multi-scale experimental ensembles and is validated through a pre-trained, experimentally benchmarked stability predictor.

BACKGROUND: The rational design of "molecular chaperone" therapeutics that selectively stabilize a target protein's native fold remains a grand challenge for protein misfolding disorders. Current generative methods lack integration of experimental data on protein dynamics and are not guided by predictors rigorously validated on real biophysical measurements.

APPROACH: A conditional 3D equivariant diffusion model will be trained on PDB complexes but conditioned on a multi-scale input: an ensemble constrained by experimental data (NMR, HDX, cryo-EM) of the misfolded/unstable state *and* the known native structure. Generation will be optimized via reinforcement learning using a pre-trained Conformational Stability Predictor, a graph neural network fine-tuned and validated on a curated dataset of small molecules with experimentally measured ΔΔG values from thermal shift assays.

EXPERIMENT: The framework will be tested on a target like transthyretin, generating molecules scored by the predictor and validated through MD simulations. Top candidates will be synthesized only after *in vitro* stabilization and selectivity are confirmed via thermal shift assays and analytical ultracentrifugation with purified protein, prior to cellular functional rescue assays.

NOVELTY: This work integrates multi-scale experimental data directly as generative constraints and employs a stability predictor pre-validated on real biophysical data, creating a closed-loop, physics-informed design cycle specifically for conformational stabilization, distinct from generic binding affinity or molecule generation.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: Develop a Pareto-aware diffusion model for molecular generation that integrates robust, uncertainty-qualified property predictors and synthetic feasibility to directly produce candidates optimized for multi-target and pharmacokinetic trade-offs.

BACKGROUND: Current generative models for polypharmacology treat multi-objective optimization as a simplistic weighted sum or sequential filter, failing to capture complex trade-offs between efficacy, selectivity, and ADMET properties. This results in molecules that are theoretically designed but often impractical due to unrealistic property combinations or synthetic intractability.

APPROACH: Implement a conditional graph diffusion model where the conditioning signal is a hybrid of discrete, high-fidelity property predictions and an uncertainty-aware context vector. The training objective will incorporate a Pareto-ranking loss to bias generation toward optimal trade-off surfaces, and a learned synthetic accessibility penalty will be applied during the denoising process to ensure realistic outputs.

EXPERIMENT: Validate first on established multi-objective benchmarks using held-out data, measuring the hypervolume and diversity of the generated Pareto front. Then, execute a focused experimental test by generating, synthesizing, and profiling 20-30 molecules for a defined kinase polypharmacology profile, comparing success rates against a controlled baseline model using identical property predictors.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond single-point conditioning to explicit Pareto-frontier exploration and directly bakes synthetic feasibility and predictive uncertainty into the core generative process, aligning the model with the practical constraints of multi-parameter drug discovery.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA: Develop a hybrid climate model by surgically replacing the high-cost cloud microphysics parameterization in a low-resolution global model with a neural operator trained on high-resolution cloud-resolving model data, explicitly bridged across scales and constrained by physical laws to ensure stable, long-term performance.

BACKGROUND: Current deep learning emulators for climate models often act as black boxes, struggling with extrapolation and losing physical interpretability. A critical bottleneck is the parameterization of sub-grid cloud microphysics, which is computationally expensive and crucial for credible climate feedbacks.

APPROACH: A Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) will be trained to emulate a high-fidelity microphysics scheme using column data from a cloud-resolving model. For insertion into a coarse global model, the operator's architecture will incorporate invariant physical constraints (e.g., conservation of mass) and its training will use a conditioning layer that statistically represents subgrid variability from the high-resolution data, ensuring stable coupling to the host dynamical core.

EXPERIMENT: The hybrid model's multi-decadal simulations will be benchmarked against the standard low-resolution model with its native physics and a pure black-box emulator, using metrics of climate mean state, cloud feedbacks under CO2 forcing, and extreme precipitation statistics.

NOVELTY: Unlike broad black-box emulation, this is a targeted, process-specific replacement that maintains the host model's interpretable dynamics, and unlike prior hybrid efforts, it formally addresses the scale mismatch via statistical conditioning and embeds hard physical constraints to ensure stability and causal consistency.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA: To develop and rigorously test a hybrid neural operator for oceanic mesoscale eddy parameterization that is trained on a numerically consistent inverse problem and evaluated on its ability to generalize beyond its idealized training data.

BACKGROUND: Coarse-resolution climate models rely on simplified parameterizations for oceanic mesoscale eddies, leading to biased projections. Pure data-driven emulators offer speed but often violate physical constraints and fail to generalize, creating a trust gap.

APPROACH: We will train a Fourier Neural Operator to predict the discrete sub-grid forcing needed for a specific coarse dynamical core (e.g., MOM6) to match coarse-grained high-resolution truth. Foundational physical constraints (e.g., potential vorticity conservation) will be architecturally enforced, but their necessity will be tested via ablation against an unconstrained network.

EXPERIMENT: Using a hierarchy of MITgcm simulations, we will test generalization to unseen forcing regimes and bathymetry, followed by multi-decadal stability tests in a coarse global model, evaluating both skill (heat transport) and physical consistency (conservation errors).

NOVELTY: This moves beyond hybrid emulation as an assumption to a testable hypothesis, rigorously evaluating the trade-offs between physical constraint and generalizable performance within a numerically consistent training framework.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA: Develop a climate model emulator that uses active learning and a conditioned latent diffusion model to probabilistically sample transition pathways toward tipping points, explicitly trained on strategically targeted simulations of bifurcation regions.

BACKGROUND: Current deep learning emulators fail to capture the low-probability, high-impact dynamics of climate tipping points because they are trained on "normal" model runs and cannot generalize to rare regime shifts. The core open problem is generating statistically plausible ensembles of collapse pathways without access to a comprehensive dataset of full tipping events, which are computationally prohibitive to produce.

APPROACH: We will iteratively train a Conditional Latent Diffusion Model (CLDM) using an active learning loop. Initially, a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with physics-informed inductive biases (e.g., enforcing smooth latent trajectories) will learn a phase space from available perturbed-parameter ensembles. The CLDM, conditioned on external forcings treated as bifurcation parameters, will then be trained. Its high-uncertainty predictions near inferred metastable boundaries will trigger new, short, and strategically initialized full-physics model runs to enrich the training set with transition dynamics, progressively refining the emulator.

EXPERIMENT: We will validate the emulator using a hierarchy of models: 1) on a conceptual model (e.g., a double-well potential) to verify it recovers the correct bifurcation diagram and transition statistics, and 2) on a low-resolution Earth System Model (e.g., FAMOUS) for partial AMOC weakening scenarios, using metrics of physical consistency (e.g., meridional heat transport) and probabilistic forecast reliability for unseen forcing pathways.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond deterministic regression by combining generative AI for stochastic transitions with an active learning framework to solve the rare-event data problem, and it rigorously grounds the latent diffusion architecture in dynamical systems theory as a learnable stochastic parameterization of unresolved bifurcation dynamics.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA: Develop a hybrid neural operator that directly replaces the most computationally expensive components of an existing GCM cloud microphysics scheme, trained via offline column emulation and validated through a stepwise online integration pathway.

BACKGROUND: Cloud microphysics parameterizations are a major computational bottleneck in climate models due to their complex, high-frequency nonlinearities. Current deep learning emulators often struggle with long-term stability and physical consistency when trained on idealized data or tasked with replacing entire subroutines.

APPROACH: We will train a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) to emulate the full tendencies of a trusted, complex microphysics scheme (e.g., a double-moment scheme) using its own offline single-column model outputs as training data. The FNO will be architecturally constrained to replace only the scheme's iterative solver core, preserving its wrapper for enforcing conservation laws. This hybrid will be integrated into the host GCM via a high-efficiency inference interface.

EXPERIMENT: Performance will be validated through a staged online protocol: 1) single-column model tests, 2) 5-day global forecast tests from ERA5 initial conditions, and 3) seasonal hindcasts. Metrics include process-level skill scores, conservation errors, and timing profiles against the original scheme within the same model infrastructure.

NOVELTY: This work moves beyond black-box emulation or correction of simplified physics by performing a targeted, numerically stable replacement of a verified scheme's bottleneck, enabled by a disciplined training and incremental coupling strategy that ensures operational relevance.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA: Develop a hybrid neural operator that couples a deterministic Fourier Neural Operator for large-scale dynamics with a stochastic generative network, trained on a strategically sampled SP-CAM dataset and constrained by physical laws, to emulate sub-grid convective cloud fields for stable, physically credible climate model acceleration.

BACKGROUND: The dominant cost and uncertainty in climate models is sub-grid cloud and convection parameterization. Current deep learning emulators act as black boxes, failing to generalize to novel climates and lacking interpretable, physically-constrained representations of organized convective structures.

APPROACH: We will generate a targeted 20-year SP-CAM dataset, actively sampled to over-represent diverse convective regimes, to train a two-part model. A Conditional Diffusion Model, explicitly conditioned on coarse environmental profiles, will generate 3D cloud fields; it will be coupled from the start to a Fourier Neural Operator via a hybrid training protocol that includes strong physical loss penalties (e.g., on column-integrated moisture and energy conservation) to ensure coupling stability.

EXPERIMENT: We will test via a tiered ablation: first, an offline-to-online test feeding the generator into fixed SP-CAM states, then a full coupled evaluation under abrupt 4xCO2 forcing using independent physical metrics like top-of-atmosphere radiative balance, spectral kinetic energy fluxes, and the progression of the Madden-Julian Oscillation.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond monolithic emulation by explicitly separating dynamics and stochastic convection, and beyond "perfect model" validation by enforcing stability through hybrid training and evaluating on independent physical plausibility metrics rather than just replication fidelity.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA: To investigate whether imposing a tunable computational cost on internal representations, alongside a severe bandwidth limit, causes multi-agent systems to develop communication protocols that actively restructure and simplify their conceptual world models for robust generalization.

BACKGROUND: Current research on emergent communication focuses on bandwidth constraints but neglects the cognitive cost of processing information. This leaves open whether pressure on an agent's internal computational resources, in tandem with communication limits, catalyzes a deeper co-adaptation of concepts and symbols, moving beyond efficient labeling to fundamental representational change.

APPROACH: We will train agents in a referential game with cluttered visual scenes under two orthogonal constraints: a limited message length and a tunable penalty on complex internal activations (e.g., L1 on feature maps). To test for conceptual restructuring, we will systematically decode internal representations against human-interpretable visual attributes (shape, color, texture). To isolate the protocol's role, we will "transplant" the emergent language between agents with frozen, capable visual systems to test generalization on novel objects.

EXPERIMENT: We will measure conceptual alignment via representational similarity and the linear decodability of visual attributes from messages. Generalization will be tested by evaluating transplanted protocols on held-out object categories, with performance collapse indicating language robustness.

NOVELTY: This introduces a tunable in-training processing cost to cleanly study dual constraints, uses attribute-based decoding to ground "conceptual compression," and employs protocol transplantation to isolate the language's causal contribution to generalization.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA: We propose to study the emergence of compositional communication by imposing a structured bandwidth constraint that forces agents to transmit primitive concepts during training and recombine them for novel composite tasks during evaluation.

BACKGROUND: A key open problem in emergent communication is whether compositional and generative codes can arise from functional pressures alone, rather than being explicitly trained. Prior work often uses holistic signals for holistic tasks, making it ambiguous whether true compositionality or mere efficient hashing has emerged.

APPROACH: We will train cooperative agents in a procedurally generated 3D world where a "planner" agent must communicate a multi-step goal to an "executor." The critical design is a *structured bottleneck*: during training, the planner transmits a fixed-length sequence of symbols, where each symbol position is semantically restricted to a specific primitive concept (e.g., *action*, *location*, *object*). The executor must learn to interpret and execute the combined instruction.

EXPERIMENT: Success is measured via zero-shot generalization to novel, logically valid combinations of primitives unseen during training. We employ rigorous baselines, including a holistic signaling condition and a non-compositional concept-scrambled condition, to isolate the causal role of the structured pressure for recombination.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond post-hoc analysis of emergent codes by designing the training environment and communication bottleneck to *require* compositionality for generalization, providing a direct test of the functional conditions for generative language-like structure.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA: To investigate the emergence of abstract conceptual communication, we will train cooperative multi-agent systems where a sender must compress high-dimensional observations into an extremely low-bandwidth continuous channel (1-10 scalars), systematically testing the hypothesis that severe bottlenecks force the development of efficient, causal conceptual tokens rather than iconic signals.

BACKGROUND: A key open problem in emergent communication is understanding how structured conceptual representations arise from environmental pressures, not just architectural biases. Most work uses discrete channels with small but sufficient vocabularies, leaving it unclear how abstraction scales under radical information constraints where one-to-one referential mapping is impossible.

APPROACH: We will use deep reinforcement learning in a series of calibrated cooperative foraging tasks where the receiver’s partial view is necessary but insufficient for optimal performance. The sender’s channel bandwidth will be systematically varied (1, 2, 5, 10 scalars). We will analyze the protocol using causal interventions—like clamping signals while varying world states—to test if signals function as discrete conceptual tokens that invariantly modulate the receiver’s policy.

EXPERIMENT: Performance will be measured via task success, with protocol analysis employing targeted causal interventions and mutual information decomposition to establish the conceptual specificity and causal efficacy of signals, compared against no-communication and sufficient-bandwidth baselines.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond correlative analysis to establish causal, functional criteria for conceptual tokens, and systematically isolates the effect of extreme bandwidth constraints as a driver for abstraction, rather than predefined inductive biases.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA: To rigorously test whether extreme bandwidth constraints force multi-agent systems to invent efficient, abstract "conceptual compression" protocols, where a single low-dimensional signal triggers a complex, context-dependent sequence of cooperative behaviors.

BACKGROUND: A key open problem in emergent communication is understanding the origins of efficient, compositional, and abstract languages. Prior work often provides agents with sufficient bandwidth, but the fundamental pressure for abstraction may only emerge under severe information bottlenecks, pushing agents beyond naming objects toward compressing holistic plans and relational concepts.

APPROACH: We will train cooperative agents in a sequential, partially-observable grid-world task using a full factorial design, independently varying communication bandwidth (2D vs. 32D vector) and signaling schedule (once per episode vs. per timestep). This isolates the bottleneck's effect. We will implement mandatory controls: an ablated channel baseline and a channel shuffling test to prove the signal's causal role.

EXPERIMENT: We will test for conceptual compression via (1) systematic generalization to novel *compositions* of task sub-goals, and (2) intervention studies that perturb the signal to alter long-horizon receiver behavior, paired with probing classifiers. Success requires the low-dimensional, per-episode condition to match the performance of high-bandwidth controls and demonstrate recombinable, abstract signal content.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond prior work on holistic signaling by using a rigorous factorial design to isolate the bandwidth constraint and introducing systematic generalization tests to distinguish true conceptual abstraction from mere policy selection or compressed perception.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA: We propose to investigate whether multi-agent systems, under a selective pressure for efficient adaptation, will evolve a functionally distinct meta-communication channel to diagnose and reconfigure their primary task-oriented protocol in response to isolated environmental or adversarial disruptions.

BACKGROUND: A key limitation of emergent communication is its brittleness to dynamic changes. Prior work shows agents can develop robust protocols for static tasks, but it remains an open problem whether they can evolve a layered communicative system where one layer dynamically manages the other, which is a hallmark of robust natural language.

APPROACH: We will train cooperative agents with two architecturally segregated channels: a high-bandwidth primary channel for task execution and a restricted meta-channel, active only during a dedicated diagnosis period following task failure. A selective pressure for efficient adaptation is created by imposing a high cost on task failure and a low bandwidth limit on the meta-channel, making protocol reset via meta-signals more optimal than learning a single, overly complex primary protocol.

EXPERIMENT: We will test this in staged referential game environments, first introducing stochastic semantic shifts and then adversarial message corruption in separate experiments. Success is measured by the agents' recovery speed post-disruption and by rigorous causal intervention tests that demonstrate meta-signals functionally alter the interpretation of subsequent primary signals.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond studying robust single-layer protocols by rigorously testing for the emergence of a functionally distinct, task-agnostic communicative layer, driven by a theoretically-grounded pressure for efficient adaptation rather than merely layering channels.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA: To predict the scaling requirements for emergent capabilities, this research will map sharp inflection points in performance across a spectrum of operationally defined, contamination-controlled tasks, using a multi-dimensional scaling analysis to test whether these inflection points form a predictable topology that reveals fundamental ceilings for different capability classes.

BACKGROUND: Current scaling laws describe smooth average loss reduction but fail to predict the discontinuous emergence of qualitatively new abilities or where scaling yields diminishing returns on novelty. The open problem is a lack of a predictive framework that quantifies if and when scaling hits a fundamental ceiling for specific emergent capabilities, rather than just incremental gains.

APPROACH: We will train a model family on a unified corpus while systematically varying size (N), dataset diversity (mixture), and compute (C). Emergent capabilities (e.g., cross-modal inference, recursive self-correction) will be defined by batteries of dynamic, procedurally generated tasks designed to prevent memorization. We will analyze performance scaling curves to identify sharp inflection points where improvements become marginal, testing if their location is predictable from scaling dimensions.

EXPERIMENT: Inflection points will be identified using performance on our synthetic task battery, with rigorous data decontamination and canonical task variants. The scaling topology will be constructed by modeling each capability's inflection point as a function of the primary scaling variables (N, D, C, mixture).

NOVELTY: This moves beyond describing aggregate loss to mapping capability-specific scaling ceilings, and replaces vague "proto-tasks" with controlled, operationalized metrics for emergence, directly testing the hypothesis of a predictable scaling topology for novel abilities.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA: To test whether scaling ceilings for complex reasoning arise from bottlenecks in specific, mechanistically-defined sub-capacities, by measuring their independent scaling laws and interference effects within a controlled model family.

BACKGROUND: Current scaling laws are aggregate and may not predict ceilings for tasks requiring multiple reasoning steps. A core open problem is whether such ceilings are due to the saturation of fundamental, model-internal operations or due to integration failures between capacities that scale independently.

APPROACH: Using an existing, openly-scoped model family (e.g., Pythia), we will identify mechanistic correlates (e.g., activation steering vectors) for subtasks within synthetic, decomposable reasoning benchmarks. We will then measure the scaling of these correlates and their causal necessity via ablation, while testing for interference through targeted architectural and training interventions.

EXPERIMENT: We will evaluate scaling trends on a synthetic benchmark of chained tasks, using performance of ablated models and success of steering vectors as metrics to establish bottleneck correlates and test their independence across model scales.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond monolithic scaling curves by proposing a "bottleneck theory" tested via mechanistic interventions, explicitly challenging the independence of sub-capacities rather than assuming modular primitives.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA: To map distinct saturation curves for specific high-value capabilities by jointly scaling model size and the quantity of a known, high-quality data source within a fixed compute budget.

BACKGROUND: Current scaling laws predict aggregate performance but obscure how individual emergent capabilities develop. A critical open problem is whether different capabilities, like complex reasoning versus code generation, saturate at the same or different scales of compute and data, which has major implications for efficient model development.

APPROACH: We will conduct controlled pre-training studies using synthetic data mixtures, where we precisely vary the proportion of a curated, high-quality data source (e.g., a verified Python code corpus) against a large, generic background corpus. We will train a series of models of increasing size on these mixtures under an iso-compute constraint to isolate the effect of data composition.

EXPERIMENT: For a pilot on Python code generation, we will scale models from 100M to 1B parameters, training each on mixtures where the code corpus fraction varies from 0% to 10%. Performance will be evaluated on held-out benchmarks like HumanEval and MBPP, tracking the saturation point for each model size.

NOVELTY: This moves beyond monolithic scaling laws by testing the hypothesis that different capabilities have divergent scaling saturation points, using a rigorous, controlled methodology focused on data composition rather than just volume.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA: We propose to predict scaling ceilings for complex capabilities by empirically decomposing them into skill demands, measuring their individual scaling curves within existing LLMs, and identifying the "weakest link" skill that bottlenecks overall performance.

BACKGROUND: Current scaling laws predict smooth aggregate improvements but may mask domain-specific ceilings. The open problem is whether scaling limits are uniform or dictated by specific sub-skills within a composite task, and what factors (e.g., data, architecture) cause those sub-skills to plateau.

APPROACH: We will first use representation probing and causal mediation analysis on a medium-scale model to empirically identify if separable skill representations exist for a synthetic composite task. We will then measure scaling curves for each skill demand across a publicly available model family (e.g., LLaMA 2 7B-70B), and compare them to curves from ablated models trained with skill-specific data up-weighting to isolate data bottleneck effects.
